source_text: Ἴδωμεν δὲ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς τῷ Κέλσῳ λεγόμενα. ἐν οἷς σφόδρα μὲν ἐλάχιστά ἐστι τὰ περὶ Χριστιανῶν πλεῖστα δὲ ὅσα περὶ Ἰουδαίων. φησὶν οὖν· εἰ μὲν δὴ κατὰ ταῦτα περιστέλλοιεν Ἰουδαῖοι τὸν ἴδιον νόμον, οὐ μεμπτὰ αὐτῶν, ἐκείνων δὲ μᾶλλον, τῶν καταλιπόντων τὰ σφέτερα καὶ τὰ Ἰουδαίων προσποιουμένων. εἰ δ᾿ ὥς τι σοφώτερον εἰδότες σεμνύνονταί τε καὶ τὴν ἄλλων κοινωνίαν (ὡς) οὐκ ἐξ ἴσου καθαρῶν ἀποστρέφονται, ἤδη ἀκηκόασιν ὅτι οὐδὲ τὸ περὶ οὐρανοῦ δόγμα ἴδιον λέγουσιν ἀλλ᾿, ἵνα πάντα ἐάσω, καὶ Πέρσαις, ὥς που δηλοῖ καὶ Ἡρόδοτος, πάλαι δεδογμένον. „νομίζουσι γὰρ,“ φησὶ, „Διῒ μὲν ἐπὶ τὰ ὑψηλότατα τῶν ὀρέων ἀναβαίνοντες θυσίας ἔρδειν, τὸν κύκλον πάντα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ Δία καλέοντες.“ οὐδὲν οὖν οἶμαι διαφέρειν Δία Ὕψιστον καλεῖν ἢ Ζῆνα ἢ Ἀδωναῖον ἢ Σαβαὼθ ἢ Ἀμοῦν, ὡς Αἰγύπτιοι, ἢ Παπαῖον, ὡς Σκύθαι. οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ κατὰ ταῦτα ἁγιώτεροι τῶν ἄλλων ἂν εἶεν. ὅτι περιτέμνονται· τοῦτο γὰρ Αἰγύπτιοι καὶ Κόλχοι πρότεροι· οὐδ᾿ ὅτι συῶν ἀπέχονται· καὶ γὰρ τοῦτ᾿ Αἰγύπτιοι, καὶ προσέτι αἰγῶν τε καὶ οἰῶν καὶ βοῶν (τε) καὶ ἰχθύων, καὶ κυάμων γε Πυθαγόρας τε καὶ οἱ μαθηταὶ καὶ ἐμψύχων ἁπάντων. οὐ μὴν οὐδ᾿ εὐδοκιμεῖν παρὰ τῷ θεῷ καὶ στέργεσθαι διαφόρως τι τῶν ἄλλων τούτους εἰκὸς, καὶ πέμπεσθαι μόνοις αὐτοῖς ἐκεῖθεν ἀγγέλους. οἷον δή τινα μακάρων χώραν λαχοῦσιν· ὁρῶμεν γὰρ αὐτούς τε καὶ τὴν χώραν τίνων ἠξίωνται. οὗτος μὲν οὖν ὁ χορὸς ἀπίτω δίκην ἀλαζονείας ὑποσχὼν, οὐκ εἰδὼς τὸν μέγαν θεὸν ἀλλ᾿ ὑπὸ τῆς Μωϋσέως γοητείας ὑπαχθείς τε καὶ ψευσθεὶς κἀκείνης οὐκ ἐπ᾿ ἀγαθῷ τέλει γεγονὼς μαθητής.
thought_title: Celsus denies that the Jews have anything special
pass_a_gloss: Let us see also the things said next (ἑξῆς) by Celsus. In which very least (ἐλάχιστα) are the things about Christians, but most (πλεῖστα) as much as about Jews. He says then: 'If then according to these things (κατὰ ταῦτα) the Jews should guard/cherish (περιστέλλοιεν) their own law, not blameworthy (μεμπτά) their [doings], but rather those [are blameworthy] who abandoned (καταλιπόντων) their own and lay claim to (προσποιουμένων) the things of the Jews. But if as knowing something wiser (σοφώτερον) they put on solemnity/pride (σεμνύνονται) and turn away (ἀποστρέφονται) from fellowship (κοινωνία) with others as not equally pure (καθαρός), they have already heard that not even the doctrine (δόγμα) about heaven (οὐρανός) do they speak as their own (ἴδιον), but, that I may let all go (ἐάσω), was also long ago (πάλαι) held (δεδογμένον) by the Persians, as somewhere Herodotus too shows (δηλοῖ). "For they are accustomed (νομίζουσι)," he says, "going up onto the highest of the mountains, to perform (ἔρδειν) sacrifices (θυσία) to Zeus, calling the whole circle (κύκλος) of heaven Zeus." I think then it differs nothing to call Zeus Most High (Ὕψιστος) or Zen (Ζήν) or Adonai or Sabaoth or Amoun, as Egyptians, or Papaeus, as Scythians. Nor indeed according to these things would they be holier (ἁγιώτεροι) than the others: that they are circumcised (περιτέμνονται), for Egyptians and Colchians [did] this first (πρότεροι); nor that they abstain from swine (σῦς), for Egyptians [do] this too, and besides (προσέτι) from goats and sheep and oxen and fish, and from beans (κύαμος) Pythagoras and his disciples, and from all ensouled things (ἔμψυχα). Nor indeed is it likely (εἰκός) that these are in good repute (εὐδοκιμεῖν) with God and loved (στέργεσθαι) in any way differently (διαφόρως) from the others, and that to them alone from there (ἐκεῖθεν) angels/messengers (ἄγγελοι) are sent, as if indeed (οἷον δή) having obtained by lot (λαχοῦσιν) some land (χώρα) of the blessed (μάκαρες); for we see both them and their land, of what things they have been deemed worthy (ἠξίωνται). Let this chorus (χορός) then depart (ἀπίτω), having undergone (ὑποσχών) the penalty (δίκη) of boasting (ἀλαζονεία), not knowing the great God but led on (ὑπαχθείς) and deceived (ψευσθείς) by the sorcery (γοητεία) of Moses, and having become a disciple/pupil (μαθητής) of it not for a good end (τέλος).'

pass_b_english: Let us also look at what Celsus says next. In it, very little concerns the Christians and most concerns the Jews. He says, then:

“If, then, the Jews were to guard their own law on these grounds, they are not to be blamed for it; rather, those are to be blamed who have abandoned their own ways and taken up those of the Jews. But if they pride themselves on knowing something wiser, and turn away from fellowship with others as not equally pure, they have already heard that not even their doctrine about heaven is their own; but, to pass over everything else, it was held long ago by the Persians too, as Herodotus somewhere shows. ‘For they are accustomed,’ he says, ‘to go up to the highest peaks of the mountains and offer sacrifices to Zeus, calling the whole circle of heaven Zeus’ (Herodotus 1.131). I think, then, that it makes no difference whether one calls Zeus the Most High, or Zen, or Adonai, or Sabaoth, or Amoun, as the Egyptians do, or Papaeus, as the Scythians do.

“Nor, indeed, would they be holier than the others on these grounds: because they are circumcised, for the Egyptians and the Colchians did this before them; nor because they abstain from swine, for the Egyptians do this too, and besides that they abstain from goats and sheep and oxen and fish; and Pythagoras and his disciples abstain from beans, and from everything that has a soul. Nor is it likely that these people are in good standing with God or loved by him in any way differently from the others, or that angels are sent from there to them alone, as though they had been allotted some land of the blessed. For we see what both they and their land have been thought worthy of.

“So let this band depart, having paid the penalty for its boasting. It did not know the great God, but was led astray and deceived by the sorcery of Moses, and it became a pupil of that sorcery to no good end.”
notes: The whole section after 'He says, then' is Celsus's text; it is set in double quotation marks (opening marks at each new paragraph by English convention), with Herodotus's sentence inside it in single marks. Herodotus 1.131 is quoted almost word for word (νομίζουσι Διὶ μὲν ἐπὶ τὰ ὑψηλότατα τῶν ὀρέων ἀναβαίνοντες θυσίας ἔρδειν, τὸν κύκλον πάντα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ Δία καλέοντες). Celsus's other material also draws on Herodotus (circumcision among Egyptians and Colchians, 2.104; Egyptian avoidance of swine, 2.47; Amoun as the Egyptian name of Zeus, 2.42; Papaeus as the Scythian Zeus, 4.59), but he does not quote these, so they are not cited inline. 'κατὰ ταῦτα' refers back to Celsus's principle in 5.25-34 that each nation rightly keeps its ancestral customs. '(ὡς)' is an editorial supplement in the staged text; '(τε)' after βοῶν likewise. The punctuation of the staged text (period before οἷον δή, period before 'ὅτι περιτέμνονται') is followed in sense but joined into English sentences. 'ἐκεῖθεν' ('from there') = from heaven / God's realm; kept literal. ἀλαζονεία rendered 'boasting'; γοητεία 'sorcery'. 'δίκην ὑποσχών' read as 'having paid the penalty' (Celsus probably alludes to the Jewish defeats under Titus and Hadrian, which Origen does not mention here). 'κἀκείνης ... μαθητής': ἐκείνης refers to γοητεία, i.e. a pupil of Moses' sorcery; reviewer changed 'his pupil' to 'a pupil of that sorcery' to keep the Greek referent (Origen's own paraphrase in 5.42, μαθητευθέντων αὐτῷ, is where Moses becomes the teacher). χορός rendered 'band' rather than the stage word 'chorus'. ἔμψυχα rendered 'everything that has a soul' (not 'living things', which would include the beans). τίνων ἠξίωνται has αὐτούς τε καὶ τὴν χώραν as its proleptic subject: 'we see what both they and their land have been thought worthy of'. Δία Ὕψιστον καλεῖν could also be read 'to call the Most High Zeus'; the list of names stands either way, so the literal order is kept. 'Zen' (Ζήν) is a poetic form of the name Zeus. Divine names here are reported names; 'God' is capitalised only in 'the great God' and 'with God', where Celsus speaks of the supreme God.
Open doubt (review): 5.41: 'Δία Ὕψιστον καλεῖν' could be read 'call the Most High Zeus' as well as 'call Zeus the Most High'; literal order kept, noted
